africanus-cesti: Julius Africanus's Miscellanies: history, science and craft, in the fragments that survive, with books 7, 2 and 3 in full and parts of books 4, 8, 9 and 13.
alexander-monachus-inventio-crucis-epito: Alexander the Monk tells how Constantine turned the empire from idols and called the Council of Nicaea, how Helena found the Cross, and why its feast is kept.
ammonius-fragmenta-joannem: Short notes on the whole of John's Gospel, from the Word in the beginning to Peter restored, defending the Trinity against the heresies along the way.
apollinaris-fragmenta-joannem: Notes on John's Gospel on the Word made flesh, the Baptist's witness, the Good Shepherd, Christ's pierced side, and Peter's threefold confession of love.
apollinaris-fragmenta-matthaeum: Notes on Matthew, from why Matthew's and Luke's genealogies differ to the Passover, the death of Judas, and the Resurrection.
apollinaris-fragmenta-psalmos: Notes on the Psalms that read them as speaking of Christ's suffering and rising, the calling of the nations, and the hope of bodily resurrection.
apollinaris-fragmenta-romanos: Notes on Romans, chiefly on faith and the Law in Abraham, the work of the Spirit, God's mercy to Israel and the nations, and the weak conscience.
arethas-epigrammata: Verse epitaphs by Arethas: a young widow named Anna mourns her early death and is praised, and a woman named Febronia is remembered for her kindness to the poor.
crocius-syntagma: Ludwig Crocius's System of Sacred Theology (Bremen, 1636), all four books: theology and its rule in Scripture; man's last end, death and the resurrection; God, the Trinity, creation, providence and sin; and the grace of Christ, the Word and sacraments, faith, the Christian life and prayer.
cyril-ad-carthaginiense: Cyril's short reply to the bishops gathered at Carthage, sending them faithful copies of the Council of Nicaea's decisions and the coming date of Easter.
cyril-adoration-1: In dialogue with Palladius, Cyril shows that the Law is a shadow of Christ, reading Abraham, Lot, and the Exodus as the soul's escape from sin.
cyril-adoration-17: Cyril reads Passover, Pentecost, the Day of Atonement, Tabernacles, and the other feasts of the Law as pictures of Christ and the age to come.
cyril-adoration-2: Cyril argues that justification comes through Christ, not the Law, reading Moses at the burning bush and the signs God gave him as figures of Christ.
cyril-adoration-3: Cyril follows Israel through the Red Sea and the battle with Amalek, reading them as baptism and the Cross, and teaches that all justification is in Christ.
cyril-adoration-4: Cyril urges the redeemed to fight sin bravely, reading Israel's census, the war on Midian, and the sharing of the spoils as lessons for the Church.
cyril-adoration-5: Cyril on courage in Christ, drawn from Achan's theft, the spies sent into Canaan, the bitter water at Marah, and the people who craved meat in the desert.
cyril-adoration-6: Cyril on loving God alone: against idols, omens, fortune-telling, belief in fate, and false oaths, with a close look at Saul and the medium of Endor.
cyril-adoration-7: Cyril on love of neighbor in the Law: the Ten Commandments, the Sabbath kept in Christ, honoring parents, and taking care not to make a brother stumble.
cyril-adoration-8: Cyril reads the Law's rules on theft, slaves, lost animals, the poor, and the cities of refuge as lessons in love for fellow believers.
cyril-adoration-9: Cyril reads the tabernacle in the wilderness, with its ark, table, lampstand, altars, and curtains, as a picture of Christ and his Church.
cyril-de-synagogae-defectu: A short piece in which Cyril finds the Trinity hidden in God's renaming of Abram as Abraham, reading the name letter by letter.
cyril-epistula-photium: A single sentence from Cyril: if two natures of different kinds were blended into one mixture, neither would survive and both would be lost.
cyril-fragmenta-acta-catholicas: Notes on Acts and the general letters, on the gifts of the Spirit at Pentecost, faith and works, guarding the tongue, hospitality, and love.
cyril-fragmenta-contra-diodorum: A short passage from a homily of Cyril on what Christ meant when he said that no one, not even the Son, knows the day or the hour.
cyril-fragmenta-contra-theodorum-2: A short passage in which Cyril argues against Theodore's followers that Christ is one and the same, both God and man, and not divided.
cyril-fragmenta-danielem: A few lines on Daniel 7, explaining that the Son coming to the Ancient of Days means entering the Father's glory, not moving through space.
cyril-fragmenta-hebraeos: Notes on Hebrews, chiefly on Christ as the eternal Son above the angels, his taking flesh to be our high priest, and the faith of Noah and others.
cyril-fragmenta-jeremiam: A few pages on Jeremiah, on Israel's idol worship on the hills, the prophet's grief for Jerusalem, and the empty wisdom of the worldly wise.
cyril-fragmenta-numeros: A few lines on Numbers: the Levites' tithe given to Aaron as a type of Christ, and the rock in the desert as a figure of Christ.
cyril-fragmentum-baruch: A few broken lines on Baruch 3:3, setting God's Wisdom, who stays unshaken, against made things, which are always perishing.
cyril-fragmentum-papyraceum: Cyril declares Apollinarius and Nestorius guilty of one and the same error, holds to the Nicene Creed, and condemns those who stir up the churches.
cyril-fragmentum-proverbia: A few lines on "The Lord created me" in Proverbs 8:22, which Cyril says means "appointed me" when said of the Son's divinity.
cyril-fragmentum-psalmum: Short notes on the Psalms: why sinners who rise again stand apart from the righteous, and how the Son made flesh stays the Father's own Son.
cyril-jerusalem-homilia-ego-vado: A brief passage from a homily on "I am going to my Father," showing that Christ says "I" of both his divinity and his humanity as one person.
cyril-matthew-fragments: Cyril of Alexandria's short notes on Matthew's Gospel, kept in later chains of comments, in the order of Matthew's chapters and verses.
cyril-recta-fide-arcadia: Cyril's treatise on the right faith for the princesses Arcadia and Marina: one Son, the Word made flesh, not two Christs.
cyril-recta-fide-pulcheria: Cyril's treatise on the right faith for the empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia: one Son, who suffers in the flesh yet as God cannot suffer.
cyril-sermo-trium-puerorum: Cyril honors Ananias, Azarias, and Misael as martyrs who confessed Christ before he came in the flesh, and ends with a prayer for the Church.
cyril-solutiones-vat-447: A few questions on Scripture, mostly without their answers: whether the rich man and Lazarus really happened, Hosea's marriage, and where Melchizedek came from.
didymus-commentarii-ecclesiasten: Didymus the Blind reads Ecclesiastes verse by verse: wealth and its cares, life as a shadow, mourning, wisdom and folly, and the fear of God.
didymus-commentarii-job: Didymus the Blind reads Job closely: the devil's envy and attacks, Job's patience, the mistakes of his friends, and God's providence in suffering.
didymus-commentarii-psalmos: Didymus the Blind reads the Psalms as the voice of Christ, explaining God's unchanging nature, the Son's divinity and humanity, and the life of virtue.
didymus-commentarii-zacchariam: Didymus the Blind explains Zechariah verse by verse, from the measuring of Jerusalem and the high priest's filthy garments to the lampstand and flying sickle.
diodorus-fragmenta-romanos: Notes on Romans, chiefly on Adam and the law of nature, the Law that exposes sin, adoption and election, and the calling of the nations.
epiphanius-de-prophetarum-vita-et-obitu-: Where each prophet came from and where each died, in a second ancient version of the work credited to Epiphanius of Salamis.
epiphanius-fragmenta-precationis-et-exor: A short prayer under the name of Epiphanius, calling on God and ordering an unclean spirit to fear him, and ending in praise.
epiphanius-testamentum-ad-cives: Epiphanius charges his people to hold fast to tradition and bring no images into churches, cemeteries, or homes, but keep God in their hearts.
epiphanius-tractatus-contra-eos-qui-imag: Epiphanius argues against painting images of Christ, the Mother of God, the saints, and the angels, saying they dishonor those they mean to honor.
epiphanius-tractatus-de-numerorum-myster: Epiphanius on faith, the Trinity, and the meaning of numbers in Scripture, listing its threes, sixes, and sevens from Genesis to the Gospels.
eusebius-emesa-fragmenta-romanos: Notes on Romans 7, arguing that "wretched man that I am" is Paul speaking in an assumed voice, and that the sin living in us is the devil.
eustathius-allocutio-constantinum: An address thanking Constantine and urging the Council of Nicaea against Arius, credited to Eustathius of Antioch but printed among works not by him.
eustathius-hexaemeron: A commentary on the six days of creation, credited to Eustathius of Antioch but printed among works not by him.
gennadius-fragmenta-corinthios: A few notes on Corinthians: Israel's cloud and sea crossing as types of baptism, faith as a spiritual gift, and one line on 2 Corinthians 10:7.
gennadius-fragmenta-galatas: A few notes on Galatians: Christ as the one mediator for all nations, the Law as a wall until faith came, and what the "elemental principles" are.
gennadius-fragmenta-hebraeos: A few notes on Hebrews: God speaking in the Son, the Son as the Father's radiance, the first teachings of the faith, and the tabernacle's symbols.
gennadius-fragmentum-2thess: A few lines on 2 Thessalonians 2: the lawless one will appear at once when God's set time ends and what holds him back is removed.
georgius-peccator-hymnus: A short prayer in verse by George, who calls himself a sinner, asking Christ to free him from his passions and let him see Christ's light and sing.
hesychius-homilia-i-hypapante: Hesychius preaches on the Presentation of Christ in the Temple as the feast of feasts, with Simeon's song and the sign spoken against as the Cross.
hesychius-homilia-i-lazarum: A short passage from Hesychius comparing Bethlehem with Zion, then praising James, the Lord's brother, for his ruling at the council in Jerusalem.
hesychius-homilia-i-longinum: Hesychius tells of Longinus, the centurion who said at the Cross "Truly this was the Son of God," and of how he was later put to death for Christ.
hesychius-homilia-i-maria-deipara: Hesychius gathers the titles and images given to Mary the God-bearer, then speaks of her virgin conception, Emmanuel in the manger, and the Incarnation.
hesychius-homilia-ii-hypapante: Hesychius on the Presentation of the infant Jesus: Simeon's welcome and prophecy, the cross as a sign spoken against, and the prophetess Anna.
hesychius-homilia-ii-lazarum: Hesychius on the raising of Lazarus, the envy of those who then plotted to kill him, and the final judgment when all the dead will rise.
hesychius-homilia-ii-longinum: Hesychius praises Longinus the centurion: his call at Christ's birth, his trials and martyrdom, and the widow healed after she recovered his head.
hesychius-homilia-ii-maria-deipara: Hesychius on Mary the God-bearer: her reply to Gabriel, the Magi, a reproach of those who rejected Christ despite His miracles, and the prophecies of Him.
hesychius-homilia-jejunio: Hesychius teaches that true fasting means abstaining from evil, joined to prayer and almsgiving, with good and bad fasts from Nineveh to Moses.
hesychius-in-antonium: Hesychius praises Antony the monk, setting him beside Abraham, Moses, David, the Baptist and Paul, and holding up his self-denial and victory over the devil.
hesychius-in-conceptionem-praecursoris: Hesychius praises John the Baptist as Forerunner, then tells of his baptizing Jesus and of Herod's oath, the girl's dance, and John's beheading.
hesychius-in-lucam: Hesychius praises Luke the evangelist for telling the whole mystery of the Incarnation, from Gabriel's greeting to the virgin birth.
hesychius-in-petrum-paulum: Hesychius praises Peter and Paul together, then retells Christ's words to Saul on the road and his turn from persecutor to apostle.
hesychius-in-procopium: Hesychius praises the martyr Procopius, comparing him to heroes of Scripture, and urges his hearers to endure persecution without fear.
hesychius-in-sanctos-martyres: A short sermon urging hearers to gather every virtue, not one, since fasting needs prayer, prayer needs almsgiving, and faith needs love.
john-damascus-de-partibus-animae: John of Damascus's short outline of the soul: its three parts, the four virtues, three kinds of love, and five powers from intellect to sense.
john-damascus-de-theologia: John of Damascus sums up the faith in brief: one God in three Persons, each with a distinct property, and two natures in the one Person of Christ.
john-damascus-de-unione: John of Damascus lists twelve kinds of union, from wine mixed with water to union in one person, to show how Christ's two natures are joined.
john-damascus-fragmenta-in-lucam: A brief note by John of Damascus on why Christ is said to baptize with fire: the tongues of fire on the apostles, or the punishing fire to come.
john-damascus-homiliae-in-dormitionem: John of Damascus's three sermons on the falling asleep of Mary, preached at her tomb at Gethsemane: praise of the Mother of God, the story of her last days and burial, and the old account in which Juvenal of Jerusalem tells the empress Pulcheria that the apostles found the tomb empty.
john-damascus-quid-est-homo: John of Damascus answers what a human being is, with a short account of the four humors, their seats in the body, temperaments, and stages of life.
john-wesley-a-caution-against-bigotry: On Mark 9:38-39: do not forbid someone who casts out devils in Christ's name just because he does not follow with us.
john-wesley-awake-thou-that-sleepest: Charles Wesley's 1742 Oxford sermon on Ephesians 5:14, which John printed: a call to those asleep in their sins to wake and come to Christ.
john-wesley-catholic-spirit: On 2 Kings 10:15, “Is your heart right, as my heart is with your heart?”: love toward Christians who differ in opinion and in ways of worship.
john-wesley-christian-perfection: On Philippians 3:12: in what sense Christians are not perfect, and in what sense they are.
john-wesley-justification-by-faith: On Romans 4:5: what justification is and is not, who is justified, and why faith is the one condition of pardon.
john-wesley-on-sin-in-believers: On 2 Corinthians 5:17: does sin remain in those who are in Christ? Wesley answers that it remains, though it no longer reigns.
john-wesley-original-sin: On Genesis 6:5: against flattering pictures of human nature, the Bible's account of a heart that is evil until God renews it.
john-wesley-salvation-by-faith: Wesley's 1738 Oxford sermon on Ephesians 2:8: what saving faith is, and how it saves from guilt, fear and the power of sin now.
john-wesley-satans-devices: On 2 Corinthians 2:11: how Satan tries to damp the joy and peace of believers pressing on to holiness, and how to resist him.
john-wesley-scriptural-christianity: Preached at Oxford in 1744 on Acts 4:31: Christianity as it began at Pentecost, as it spread, and as it will one day fill the earth, with a hard look at Oxford itself.
john-wesley-the-almost-christian: Preached at Oxford in 1741 on Acts 26:28: the gap between being almost a Christian and being one altogether, in love of God, love of neighbor and faith.
john-wesley-the-circumcision-of-the-hear: Preached at Oxford on 1 January 1733 on Romans 2:29: the holiness of heart God asks for, in humility, faith, hope and love.
john-wesley-the-first-fruits-of-the-spir: On Romans 8:1: who are in Christ Jesus, how they walk after the Spirit, and why there is no condemnation for them.
john-wesley-the-great-assize: Preached at Bedford in 1758 on Romans 14:10: the signs before the Last Judgment, the judgment itself, and how to be ready to stand there.
john-wesley-the-great-privilege-of-those: On 1 John 3:9: what it means to be born of God, how it differs from being justified, and why whoever is born of God does not commit sin.
john-wesley-the-kingdom-of-god-is-at-han: On Mark 1:15: the kingdom of God is not rites or right opinions but righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Ghost, near to all who repent and believe.
john-wesley-the-law-established-through-: On Romans 3:31: the ways preachers make the law void through faith, starting with not preaching it at all.
Wesley's second sermon on Romans 3:31: how we establish the law by what we teach and by how we live, since faith works by love.
john-wesley-the-lord-our-righteousness: On Jeremiah 23:6: what the righteousness of Christ is, how it is counted to believers, and a plea for peace among those who argue over the words.
john-wesley-the-marks-of-the-new-birth: On John 3:8: the marks of those born of the Spirit: faith with power over sin, hope, and love.
john-wesley-the-means-of-grace: On Malachi 3:7: whether there are means of grace, what they are, and how to use prayer, Scripture and the Lord's Supper without trusting in them.
john-wesley-the-nature-of-enthusiasm: On Acts 26:24: what enthusiasm, or religious madness, is, the forms it takes, and how to avoid it without losing true religion.
john-wesley-the-original-nature-property: On Romans 7:12: where the moral law came from, why it is holy, just and good, and what it is for.
john-wesley-the-repentance-of-believers: On Mark 1:15, closed at Londonderry in 1767: why believers still need to repent of the pride, self-will and sin that remain in them.
john-wesley-the-righteousness-of-faith: On Romans 10:5-8: the righteousness of the law set against the righteousness of faith, and why no one can build on their own obedience.
john-wesley-the-scripture-way-of-salvati: On Ephesians 2:8: what salvation is, what faith is, and how we are saved by it, from pardon to holiness of heart.
john-wesley-the-spirit-of-bondage-and-of: On Romans 8:15: three states of the soul, the natural man asleep, the man under the law in fear, and the child of God set free.
john-wesley-the-witness-of-our-own-spiri: On 2 Corinthians 1:12: the witness of a good conscience, living in simplicity and godly sincerity by the grace of God.
john-wesley-the-witness-of-the-spirit-di: On Romans 8:16: how God's Spirit bears witness with ours that we are His children, and how to tell that witness from a delusion.
Wesley's second sermon on Romans 8:16, written years after the first: what the witness of the Spirit is, and answers to those who deny it.
john-wesley-upon-our-lords-sermon-on-the: The first of thirteen sermons on the Sermon on the Mount, on Matthew 5:1-4: who is speaking, whom He teaches, and the poor in spirit and those who mourn.
The second sermon on the Sermon on the Mount, on Matthew 5:5-7: the meek, those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, and the merciful.
The third sermon on the Sermon on the Mount, on Matthew 5:8-12: the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those persecuted for righteousness' sake.
The fourth sermon on the Sermon on the Mount, on Matthew 5:13-16: Christians as salt and light, and why Christianity is a social religion that cannot be hidden.
The ninth sermon on the Sermon on the Mount, on Matthew 6:24-34: no one can serve God and mammon, so take no anxious thought and seek first the kingdom of God.
The fifth sermon on the Sermon on the Mount, on Matthew 5:17-20: Christ came to fulfill the law, not to destroy it, and the righteousness that exceeds the Pharisees'.
The sixth sermon on the Sermon on the Mount, on Matthew 6:1-15: giving and praying in secret, the Lord's Prayer, and a pure intention in all we do.
The seventh sermon on the Sermon on the Mount, on Matthew 6:16-18: fasting, what it is for, how it is abused, and how to keep it.
The eighth sermon on the Sermon on the Mount, on Matthew 6:19-23: treasures on earth and in heaven, and the single eye of a pure intention.
The tenth sermon on the Sermon on the Mount, on Matthew 7:1-12: judging others, holy things and pearls, asking, seeking and knocking, and the golden rule.
The eleventh sermon on the Sermon on the Mount, on Matthew 7:13-14: the strait gate and the narrow way, and why so few find it.
The twelfth sermon on the Sermon on the Mount, on Matthew 7:15-20: beware of false prophets, and know them by their fruits.
The last of the thirteen sermons on the Sermon on the Mount, on Matthew 7:21-27: not everyone who says Lord, Lord, and the wise man who builds on the rock.
john-wesley-wandering-thoughts: On 2 Corinthians 10:5: which wandering thoughts are sinful, which are not, and which we may hope to be free from.
le-blanc-theses-theologicae: Louis Le Blanc, a Reformed professor at Sedan, sets out theology in theses argued against Rome: Scripture, faith, grace, free choice, good works and the saints.
oecumenius-fragmenta-philippenses: Short notes on Philippians: Paul's aim to teach humility, the fruit of his chains, and why he counts his former gains as loss.
oecumenius-fragmenta-titum: Short notes on Titus: why Paul quotes the poet who called Cretans liars, why he orders sharp rebuke, and how all things are pure to the pure.
oecumenius-fragmentum-philemonem: A few lines on the opening of Philemon: Paul names his chains first to give weight to his request for Onesimus.
olympiodorus-fragmentum-gaudete: Olympiodorus on rejoicing in suffering: as health makes hardship easy, so suffering for the truth, like Paul's and the apostles', is itself a prize.
origen-1-corinthians-fragments: Origen's notes on 1 Corinthians from start to finish: the Church, the cross and wisdom, building on Christ, marriage, love, and the rising of the dead.
origen-acta-homily-scrap: A short passage from Origen's homilies on Acts: how Peter can say the Holy Spirit spoke the Psalm about Judas, when the words seem to be Christ's.
origen-de-resurrectione-scrap: Fragments from Origen on the rising of the dead: Lazarus and the rich man, the soul's bodily form after death, and the risen being like the angels.
origen-ephesians-fragments: Origen's notes on Ephesians verse by verse, from Paul's greeting and the Church as Christ's body to husbands and wives and the armor of God.
origen-hebrews-homily-scrap: Origen judges that Hebrews holds Paul's thoughts in another's polished wording, notes claims for Clement and Luke, and says only God knows who wrote it.
origen-homilies-jeremiah: Origen on Jeremiah: all twenty homilies that survive in Greek. Two more survive only in Jerome's Latin and are not included here.
origen-job-enarrationes: Origen's notes on Job, from the hedge around him and his wife's advice through the friends' speeches to the dragon and Job's double reward.
origen-job-homilies: Origen preaches on Job as a blameless man tested, not punished: providence, God's hidden face, the dragon, and Job's double blessing.
origen-job-selecta: Selected notes by Origen on Job: the devil's raid, hard words, Elihu, God's challenge to Job, the dragon bound, and Job's double reward.
origen-lamentations-fragments: Origen on Lamentations: Jeremiah's grief for captive Jerusalem, read also as the soul taken captive by sin and set free by Christ.
origen-nt-fragments: Origen's notes on John, Luke and Matthew: the Word who was in the beginning, the Baptist, the Passion, and why the Church keeps only four Gospels.
origen-osee-fragment: Origen explains why a verse in Hosea shifts from plural to singular: those who walk with God become one, while those who sin become many.
origen-proverbs-expositio: Origen reads Proverbs as hidden sayings that teach wisdom and self-control, setting the way of virtue and knowledge against the way of wickedness.
origen-proverbs-fragments: Origen's notes on Proverbs: proverbs, dark sayings and riddles, Wisdom as Christ, and the Church moving in order like the locusts.
origen-psalms-excerpta: Origen's selected notes on the Psalms, reading Zion, the earth and the Exodus as pictures of the Church and the soul, and the psalms as speaking of Christ.
origen-psalms-fragments-greek: Origen's verse-by-verse notes on Psalms 1 to 22, read as words about Christ and as steps in the soul's progress from shunning evil to doing good.
origen-regnorum-fragments: Origen on hard passages in Samuel and Kings: Eli's sons, God's anger and repentance, David and the holy bread, and the medium of Endor.
origen-ruth-scrap: A short fragment in which Origen reads Ruth as a type of the Gentiles and asks how a Moabite could enter the assembly of God.
origen-song-commentary-liber-4: Origen on Song of Songs 2:10-15: the Bridegroom calls the soul out as winter passes, and the little foxes that spoil the vines stand for sins and heretics.
photius-bibliotheca: Photius's notes on the first 17 books in his Library, from Theodore's defense of Dionysius to the Acts of the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon.
photius-epigramma: A short verse by Photius commending the romance of Clitophon and Leucippe to readers who want to live chastely, for Leucippe's endurance.
photius-fragmentum-2tim: A single note on 2 Timothy 2:2: the faithful men are the bishops and elders Timothy would ordain, and the many witnesses are the Law and the Prophets.
photius-fragmentum-philemonem: Photius in a few lines on the opening of Philemon: Paul puts his chains first so that his request for Onesimus carries weight.
procopius-gaza-epistula: A short thank-you letter from Procopius of Gaza praising a friend's letter as a spring of words and asking him not to fall silent.
procopius-gaza-epistula-altera: A playful letter from Procopius of Gaza blaming Dionysus for a poor scholar's thin harvest, and concluding that no one is rich in both words and money.
procopius-gaza-refutatio-procli: Procopius of Gaza, answering Proclus, sets the eternal procession of the Son and Spirit from the Father apart from the processions of all created things.
severianus-fragmentum-philemonem: Severianus of Gabala in a few lines on Philemon: Paul opens with his chains to give credit to his plea for Onesimus.
theodorus-heracleensis-matthew-fragments: Theodore of Heraclea's notes on Matthew, from the genealogy and the Baptist to the Passion, often showing how Matthew agrees with Luke.
theophilus-alex-fragmenta-joannem: Theophilus says Christ's words on the man born blind refute the idea that souls live before the body and are sent into bodies for their sins.
theophilus-alex-fragmenta-matthaeum: Theophilus on the parable of the two sons: the Gentiles first refused and then repented, while Israel promised to obey and did not.
acts-of-justin: How Justin and six companions were questioned by the prefect Rusticus in Rome, condemned, and beheaded for their faith.
conon-gardener: Conon, an old gardener at Magydus who says he is from Nazareth and of Christ's family, will not sacrifice and dies after being made to run before the governor's chariot.
cyprian: The official record of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage: his questioning by the governor Paternus and exile to Curubis, then his arrest, sentence by Galerius Maximus, and death by the sword in 258.
didache: An early Christian handbook, probably from about 100: the way of life and the way of death, then teaching on baptism, fasting, prayer, the Eucharist, traveling prophets, church leaders and the Lord's return.
irenaeus: The trial of Irenaeus, bishop of Sirmium, before Probus, governor of Pannonia, in 304: he refuses to sacrifice though his family begs him, and he is put to the sword and thrown into the river Sava.
marianus-james: A friend who shared their road tells how Marian, a reader, and James, a deacon, were arrested near Cirta in Numidia, tortured, strengthened by visions in prison at Lambaesis, and beheaded by a river with many others.
maximus: The short record of Maximus, a man of Asia who gave himself up in the persecution of Decius, was questioned by the proconsul Optimus, refused to sacrifice, and was stoned outside the walls.
montanus-lucius: Lucius, Montanus, Flavian and their companions write from prison at Carthage of their arrest, hunger and visions. A fellow Christian then tells how they died and what Flavian taught the church on his last day.
perpetua-felicitas: The prison diary of Perpetua, a young mother of Carthage, with the visions of Saturus and an editor's account of how she, the slave woman Felicity and their companions died in the arena in 203.
basil-homilia-misericordia-judicio: A short homily: mercy and justice belong together, gifts to the poor must not come from money taken unjustly, and mercy shown to the poor is shown to Christ.
basil-homilia-invidia: Basil calls envy the most deadly of the passions: it eats up the envious, drove Joseph's brothers and Christ's enemies, and is cured by prizing virtue above wealth and fame.
augustine-divination-of-demons: Augustine answers pagans who said their gods foretold the fall of the temples: God may allow what he does not approve, demons foresee some things only through their keen bodies and long experience, and the prophets foretold the end of idols long before.
basil-homiliae-hexaemeron: Basil's sermons on the six days of creation in Genesis 1: Moses is a witness to trust, the world had a beginning and will have an end, God made matter itself, and evil is not a thing God made.
augustine-psalm-against-the-donatists: A song Augustine wrote about 393 for ordinary Christians to sing. It tells the story of the Donatist split and calls its people back to the one Church, which like the Lord's net holds good and bad until the end.
athanasius-epistula-maximum: Athanasius answers the philosopher Maximus: he nearly kept silent before shameless opponents, but he confesses that the one crucified is God the Word, who offered his own body to save us.
basil-homilia-in-psalmum-28: Basil's second homily on Psalm 28 (29 in Hebrew numbering): worship only within the Church, and hear the Lord's voice over the waters as John the Baptist, a voice that breaks cedars and lays hidden sins bare.
evagrius-capitula-xxxiii: Thirty-three one-line definitions by Evagrius that read the diseases, beasts and powers named in Scripture as pictures of the soul's vices, of false knowledge, and of growth toward God.
evagrius-de-magistris: Evagrius on how a spiritual father should guide his disciples: an unskilled guide destroys and a skilled one heals, correction comes without anger, and the road leads, like Israel's to Elim, to freedom from the passions.
augustine-on-faith-and-the-creed: Augustine, then a priest, explains the creed to the bishops of Africa at Hippo in 393, line by line: God made all things from nothing, the Son is not a creature, the Word took flesh, and the Spirit is equal with the Father and the Son.
didymus-fragmentum-hebraeos: A few lines on Hebrews 1 by Didymus the Blind: all creation, the angels included, worships Christ, and since Scripture forbids the worship of a creature, Christ is the Creator, who also took created flesh.
basil-homilia-gratiarum-actione: Basil on Paul's command to rejoice always and give thanks in everything: how a Christian keeps joy in loss, why Christ wept, and how Job gave thanks when all was taken from him.
severianus-fragmenta-2tim: Short notes by Severianus of Gabala on 2 Timothy: why Paul writes by command in the first letter and by promise in the second, when to rebuke and when to teach, and greed as a danger to the ministry.
cyril-homilia-cyrini: A short homily Cyril preached in the church of Cyrinus: God, who is life, made humanity for a life without decay, and the adversary plotted to undo it.
basil-in-principio-erat-verbum: Basil on the first words of John's Gospel: why John says beginning and Word rather than Son, and how the four phrases of John 1:1 guard the faith against those who make the Son a creature.
cyril-fragmenta-contra-theodorum-3: Passages from Cyril's third book against Theodore of Mopsuestia: the Godhead and the flesh keep their own properties, yet Christ is one Son, and his humanity is honored and made holy in that union.
davenant-dissertationes-duae: John Davenant argues from Scripture that Christ's death is a remedy offered to every person, so that anyone who hears the Gospel may be called to believe, and then opens a second dissertation on predestination.
basil-quod-rebus-mundanis: Preached after a fire near the church: wealth and pleasure are not truly ours, the soul has its own lasting goods, and Job shows how to endure loss.
basil-in-ebriosos: One night of drinking seems to undo seven weeks of Lenten preaching, and Basil answers it: drunkenness is a demon people choose for themselves, it wrecks body and soul, and the sober must keep apart from it.
athanasius-scholia-job: Short notes on Job. Athanasius turns the sons born to Job against the Arians, praises Job's endurance against the devil's tricks, and reads the book's mountains and signs as the prophets and the Passion.
polycarp: The church of Smyrna tells the church of Philomelium how its old bishop Polycarp was arrested, refused to curse Christ, and was burned and stabbed in the arena, in a death that followed the pattern of the Gospel.
eustathius-in-ecclesiasten: A few lines on Ecclesiastes credited to Eustathius of Antioch: here spirit means the soul, and pleasure leaves nothing behind once it has passed.
athanasius-epistula-afros: Athanasius and the bishops of Egypt and Libya write to the bishops of Africa that the creed of Nicaea is enough and the Council of Ariminum is not, and explain why Nicaea said the Son is of the Father's substance.
evagrius-rerum-monachalium: Evagrius's advice to monks: give up worldly cares for stillness, avoid distractions, fight listlessness with work, and order the day around prayer.
basil-homilia-de-spiritu-sancto: Basil preaches that the Holy Spirit is not a creature: he shares God's name and honor, gives his gifts, and brings new birth in baptism. A word on the Eucharist closes the homily.
